::: {.lead}
We are excited to announce River 1.0, the first Marketing Foundation Model from PyMC Labs, completely open source.
:::

River processes tabular marketing data, including media spend, impressions, and key
covariates, alongside business outcomes like sales to generate a posterior probabilistic
distribution about the underlying system behind your data. This provides an approximated
overview of the entire marketing ecosystem and quantifies the impact of each variable
on your target outcome.

*It’s important to note that River is a research preview*. The benchmarks use simulated data,
so we can compare estimated contributions with known values and forecasts with held-out outcomes.

## Bayesian inference, learned once {#bayesian-inference}

Traditionally, once you specify a Bayesian marketing mix model, or any Bayesian
model, a sampler such as the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) can explore its posterior.
Each draw gives a plausible combination of media effect, carryover, and
saturation parameters, conditional on the model and the data.

{{< include _sampling-space.qmd >}}

But, **what if much of that model-building work could be done once, then reused
across businesses?** Foundation models operate on this exact premise. Rather
than training a dedicated system for each individual task, a unified model is
trained once and successfully adapted across diverse applications.

## Training and Architecture {#training}

River learns a sampler for a family of specifications. A prior set of decisions
defines possible systems, and a simulator creates many datasets with known
truth. The datasets together are called our knowledge/training corpus.


::: {#architecture}
We used a transformer encoder paired with a two-stage posterior sampler
architecture. First, a router samples a graph of direct effects based on the
output from the encoder. Next, a graph conditioner adapts that output to the
specifically sampled graph, allowing a flow decoder to map noise directly into
detailed contribution draws. The flow networks themselves are trained using
conditional flow matching. In terms of specifications, the encoder features a
width of 128 alongside a feed-forward width of 512, while each flow network is
built with two 256-unit hidden layers.

{{< include _architecture.qmd >}}

```{=html}
<figure class="mfm-training-stats mfm-reveal">
  <div class="mfm-stats">
    <div><strong>2.4M</strong><span>parameters</span></div>
    <div><strong>4</strong><span>encoder blocks</span></div>
    <div><strong>8</strong><span>attention heads per block</span></div>
    <div><strong>16</strong><span>Euler steps per flow sample</span></div>
  </div>
  <figcaption>We trained River for 12 hours on one NVIDIA H100 GPU. We ran 62,500 AdamW updates with 64 views per update (3.4 epochs).</figcaption>
</figure>
```
:::

## Evaluation {#benchmarks}

Standard regression models are built to predict outcomes. River operates in a
fundamentally different paradigm: it was never trained to minimize prediction
error on a target variable.

In media mix modeling, forecasting accuracy is secondary, the true goal is
recovering the latent causal mechanisms connecting inputs to business outcomes,
a task traditional regression routinely fails to accomplish when considered in
isolation.

Because true marketing effects are unobservable in historical data. On the
other hand, simulations offer a way to objectively observe ground truth values.
Using those observations, we can directly evaluate River’s ability to uncover
true media effects.

### Design {#test-overview}

We generated five scenarios representing common real-world regression
challenges. Across each scenario, we benchmarked River against established
media mix modeling approaches, such as PyMC Marketing configured with both
time-varying and constant intercepts. In graph-averaged mode, River estimates
contributions across sampled causal graphs. In true-graph mode, we supply the
simulator's graph for the visible inputs. The reference model uses information
about the simulator's priors or structure.

We sum media and control contributions over the holdout and report signed
relative error: (truth − estimate) divided by truth. We use the visible inputs
and include indirect effects in the media total. We omit relative errors when
the magnitude of the true contribution is at or below 0.1% of mean context
sales times the number of holdout weeks. For sales forecasts, we report mean
absolute error as a share of mean context sales. We also score posterior draws
against the simulated truth using the continuous ranked probability score
(CRPS).

In the six tests with known contributions, we supply 99, 185, or 207 weeks of
sales and withhold the rest of the 208 weeks. Each method produces 1,000 draws
per supported case.

### Results {#what}

Across all experiments, a key pattern emerges: River effectively determines
when and where not to redistribute variance. Unlike traditional least-squares
regression, when a variable is absent, River does not redistribute unassigned
variance across remaining covariates to artificially improve target fit. As a
result, outcome predictions may be slightly lower than traditional methods
(-11%), but contribution decompositions remain considerably more accurate
(+74%).

These results align with our goals. In marketing analytics, they demonstrate
an alternative to traditional regression by focusing directly on the metric
that matters most: the latent causal effect hidden within the marketing
ecosystem.

Furthermore, as a pre-trained network, it entirely bypasses traditional MCMC
convergence challenges. Analysts using River no longer need to spend extensive
time manually tuning samplers just to help them navigate complex parameter
spaces effectively given by the nature of the data.

{{< include _benchmark-distributions.qmd >}}

### Speed {#speed}

By leveraging pre-trained network architectures, we amortized posterior
inference across diverse Bayesian model configurations. Like standard
amortized inference networks, because the computational cost of training is
paid upfront, subsequent evaluation becomes exceptionally fast.

In our benchmarks, River demonstrated speeds roughly 14 times faster than
traditional MCMC. To ensure a rigorous comparison, each baseline method was
evaluated using its optimal hardware configuration; for instance, running MCMC
on high-core-count CPUs when GPU data-transfer overhead would otherwise degrade
performance. Similarly, River was benchmarked on GPUs where its architecture
achieves maximum throughput. Rather than restricting all models to identical
hardware, this evaluation protocol reliably measures peak execution speed
across each method's optimal compute environment.

{{< include _speed-distributions.qmd >}}

### Causal structure {#structure}

We validate River on the cases where conditional causal discovery is viable,
specifically when evaluating input sets with varying target connections, we
benchmarked River against established frameworks such as GES and PC using the
DoWhy from Microsoft.

When testing data similar to its training set, River works well, though it
finds a few more false positives than traditional methods. However, on
completely new data formats, its accuracy drops significantly compared to
standard approaches.

{{< include _discovery-plots.qmd >}}

## Our vision for marketing measurement {#vision}

Foundational models represent the next evolution in marketing science. Rather
than forcing organizations to rely on narrow, rigid analyst assumptions and
long iteration cycles, our approach encodes a spectrum of possible marketing
dynamics into a single pre-trained model. By automatically inferring potential
structures across diverse scenarios, it consolidates years of marketing
knowledge into one transparent, unified training corpus on which the
Foundational model is trained.

River represents our initial stride toward this evolving framework, shifting
the focus of data scientists from manually crafting specific functional math
formulas toward more comprehensively mapping out the underlying ecosystem and
its full spectrum of dynamics.

## Open questions & Next steps {#open-questions}

To be clear, this architecture is not without limitations. Uncovering those
boundaries remains challenging due to how effectively the underlying network
internalizes and generalizes patterns across scenarios.

Currently, the generalizable knowledge frontier beyond our training corpus
appears non-uniform. Depending on the specific dimension under evaluation,
performance can vary from exceptional extrapolation to noticeable degradation.
A prime example is handling expanded channel counts or datasets with novel
statistical characteristics, where River continues to outperform standard
benchmarks. Crucially, these scenarios remain grounded within established
structural causal frameworks and Pearlian definitions of causality.

However, when evaluated on novel functional structures that fall outside these
core foundational boundaries, performance degrades noticeably, particularly
within the causal discovery phase. We are actively investigating these edge
cases to delineate a rigorous framework of constraints for our forthcoming
academic publication.

Looking ahead, our focus centers on expanding the diversity of functional
relationships and complex interactions incorporated within our training corpus.
By incorporating these additional scenarios, we aim to broaden the model's
overall knowledge frontier and ensure more robust coverage across unseen
environments.

{{< include _knowledge-frontier.qmd >}}

## Usage {#get}

We plan to launch River publicly during December 2026. For early access, sign
up through our [registration form](https://www.pymc-labs.com/white-papers/marketing-foundation-models#get-paper)
to join the preview cohort.

Check the [Load model introduction](../../guide/examples/river_1_quickstart.ipynb) for
loading pre-trained weights and executing inference. Dive into the
[comprehensive documentation](../../guide/training.qmd) for detailed workflows
on pre-training custom foundation architectures.

```python
import pymc_mfm as mfm

model = mfm.load(
    "river-1",
    date_column="week",
    target_column="sales",
    channel_columns=["tv", "search"],
    control_columns=["price"],
)
```

```python
import pandas as pd

# Weekly history includes sales; future weeks include media and controls.
history = pd.read_csv("history.csv", parse_dates=["week"])
future = pd.read_csv("future.csv", parse_dates=["week"])
result = model.inference(history, future, n_samples=100, random_seed=0)
result.plot.contributions_over_time()
```
